newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH FORESTRY HEAD LOOKS FOR FEBRUARY UPTURN.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH FORESTRY HEAD LOOKS FOR FEBRUARY UPTURN.

text.p: The Federation of Finnish Forest Industries' new chairman Juha Niemela said on Wednesday he expected no clear signs of an upturn before February.
Niemela is also CEO of UPM-Kymmene , Europe's biggest forest industry group.
"Most probably we won't see very good signs before, say, February," Niemela told Reuters after a news conference on the federation's autumn meeting.
His remarks came after the federation issued a report headlined "Upturn ahead" which said an increase in European growth was expected but that prospects were still uncertain.

"In the normal case the paper industry starts to live strongly again in February," Niemela said, but added that the outlook was still uncertain and that prospects for the Finnish industry hinged on trends in Finland's key trading partners.
"The forecasters betrayed us this year," he said. "They forecast about double the growth that is now materialising. Again there are ... good forecasts, but let's hope this time that they are right."
"We cannot determine better than the experts," Niemela said referring to the general economic outlook. He also declined to predict price trends for forest industry products.

The federation said in its report that pulp prices - a leading price indicator for the sector and particularly for fine papers - had not risen according to plan due to higher inventories and because of increased pulp output in Asia.
Softwood pulp prices have been hovering at about $560 to $580 per tonne for about a half a year, after rising from a trough of $480 per tonne.

"Even though the markets as such are growing very fast (in the Far East), the capacities come in very high steps, so occasionally we might see disturbances in America and Europe as well," Niemela said.
Niemela said that if pulp prices remained at their current depressed level, only the most efficient producers would survive in the long term.
Finnish producers "would be among the best", he added.
The federation said that North American and Scandinavian (Norscan) pulp inventories had risen again since the summer months and that this had dampened hopes for price rises.
Niemela told the news conference that with Norscan pulp inventories 200,000-300,000 tonnes above their equilibrium level of about 1.5 million tonnes, pulp prices remain unpredictable.
"It seems to be the kind of prickly situation from which pulp prices could in fact shoot in any direction whatsoever," he said.
Niemela also told the news conference that mill stoppages would be needed but that it was unknown whether the curtailments due at the end of the year would be enough.

"It is undeniable that Far Eastern pulp, and above all Indonesian production, has a clear impact on world prices. Staring exclusively at these so-called Norscan inventories is self-deception nowadays," Niemela added.
